Photograph: Russell Hart/Alamy Ofsted Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in Ofsted Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action Richard Adams Education editor Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tensions between England’s headteachers and Ofsted are developing into a crisis after school leadership unions said they had no confidence in the watchdog and would hold strike ballots unless “significant wellbeing issues” caused by Ofsted’s inspections regime were fixed. The Association of School and College Leaders​ (ASCL), which includes senior leaders in many secondary schools, described Ofsted’s inspection system as “an overbearing mess” and urged the government to pause inspections to stop teachers leaving the profession. A spokesperson for ASCL said that “if change is not forthcoming” the union would seek to hold an indicative ballot on industrial action. New Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey says Read more The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said it would also consider steps including strike action at a meeting of its leadership next week. The combative moves come after a survey published by Ofsted showed 88% of schools reported that recent inspections had negatively affected staff wellbeing. The Guardian reported last week that Lucy Powell, the education secretary, wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” and overhaul the framework introduced last year. The new framework was intended to lower the strain and workload caused by inspections, but many heads say the opposite has happened. In response to ASCL’s announcement, a spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “Inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face. “That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.” An Ofsted spokesperson said: “We have worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge. “We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do.” ​Hostility ​towards Ofsted has been heightened since the death of Ruth Perry, a popular headteacher in Reading. In 2023 a coroner found that an Ofsted inspection contributed to Perry’s mental health deterioration and her death. Labour pledged to reform school inspections in its 2024 election manifesto. But ASCL said it had “seen no meaningful progress on the part of Ofsted to address significant wellbeing issues caused by inspections, and that it is increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members”. England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints Read more The motion of no confidence in Ofsted passed by ASCL’s executive stated: “We fear that the disproportionate stress and anxiety exerted by the inspection system will lead to school leaders deciding to leave their posts with a consequent impact on schools, children and young people.” Pepe Di’​Iasio, ​ASCL’s general ​secretary, said: “​Our repeated attempts to resolve our concerns through discussion and negotiation have hit a brick wall … The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed.” Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the NAHT, said: “Our deep concerns about this Ofsted framework and the impact it is having on professionals are longstanding. Our executive committee will be meeting at the end of next week and debating the next steps NAHT will take. We fully expect that debate to include the option of pursuing industrial action.” Explore more on these topics Ofsted Schools Trade unions Department for Education Teachers' workload England news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students

Czech MEP Andrej Dostál supports Pakistan’s position on water treaty. German MEP Michael von der Schulenburg urges international efforts. BRUSSELS: Pakistan has urged the international community to uphold international law and respect international agreements, highlighting the Jammu and Kashmir dispute and the Indus Waters Treaty during a meeting at the European Parliament on the future of global governance. Pakistan’s Ambassador to Belgium, Luxembourg and the European Union, Rahim Hayat Qureshi, addressed the meeting, stressing that respect for international treaties was essential to global stability and the continued relevance of international law. Qureshi drew attention to Pakistan’s concerns over violations of the Indus Waters Treaty and called for the Jammu and Kashmir dispute to be resolved in accordance with relevant United Nations resolutions. He said relations between states should be based on equal rights and emphasised the importance of including the views of all relevant parties in efforts to reform the United Nations and advance the wider global interest. The ambassador also called for greater international cooperation on reforming the global financial system, tackling climate change and developing modern technologies. During the meeting, Czech Member of the European Parliament Andrej Dostál supported Pakistan’s position on the Indus Waters Treaty, while German MEP Michael von der Schulenburg urged the international community to play a role in ensuring the treaty’s implementation and compliance. The discussion comes amid continuing tensions over the treaty after India announced in April 2025 that it would hold the agreement in abeyance following an attack in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir. Pakistan has rejected the move and maintained that the treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended. The 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, governs the sharing of the Indus River system between Pakistan and India. The dispute has become a major point of contention between the two countries, with Islamabad warning that any attempt to restrict its water flows would have serious consequences. According to the energy association BDEW, Germany has been a net importer of electricity since 2023. The neighbouring countries Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, were the most important buyers of German electricity in the first nine months of 2026. Together, they bought about half of all German electricity exports. The volume of German electricity exported rose by 25.5% compared with the same period last year, to 48.8 terawatt-hours, while its value increased by 51.3% to €4.3 billion ($4.7 billion). Electricity imports into Germany fell by 13.3% in volume, but at 49.2 terawatt-hours they remained slightly above exports. While imported electricity cost an average of €116 per megawatt-hour, 39% more than a year earlier, exported electricity from Germany averaged only €87 per megawatt-hour, some 20.6% more than a year earlier. With a high share of renewable energy sources , wind and solar, Germany tends to offer electricity when supply is high and prices are low, but in times of shortage it has to pay higher prices for imported electricity. Those protests, which took place on October 31, saw tens of thousands take to the streets across Germany, with crowds remaining largely peaceful, although rioting broke out in several cities, including Frankfurt, later in the evening. Among the demands of the "Gen Z Takes Charge" group are increased funding for schools, addiction support and psychotherapy, affordable living, opposition to conscription and consistent action on climate change. Lufthansa's parent company Lufthansa Group had 67,100 employees in Germany by the end of last year. In the letter seen by news agencies, Lufthansa said financial struggles were the reason behind the planned cuts. "Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said, while pointing out that the company operated at a €180 million ($197 million) loss in the first nine months of this year. In addition, Lufthansa Airlines is now in its third straight year of being unprofitable. In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran , further complicating its financial outlook.
